newsitem.title: SPAIN: Battle over Spain pay-TV rages despite peace offer.
newsitem.headline: Battle over Spain pay-TV rages despite peace offer.

text.p: Battle for control of Spain's nascent pay television market flared again on Tuesday after Telefonica's digital platform rejected a peace offer.
Canal Satelite, a digital television group competing with Telefonica's Via Digital, said on Monday it was willing to hold talks about sharing its exclusive soccer broadcast rights.
The rights, owned by Audiovisual Sport, are seen by industry analysts as crucial to making investment-heavy digital pay television profitable in football-mad Spain.

They have been at the centre of a bitter war for months pitting the government, Telefonica and one major media group against the leading opposition Socialist party and another big media group connected to Canal Satelite.

Via Digital rejected the Canal Satelite offer, saying on Tuesday the platform controlled by France's Canal Plus and Spanish media group Prisa did not hold exclusive rights for the 1997/98 season that starts on August 30.
"We will sit down with whomever has the football rights, which is not Canal Satelite for the next season," Via Digital chairman Pedro Perez told state radio on Tuesday.
"We would be delighted to reach an agreement, which would be relatively easy -- we are talking about hours, not days -- on our part with the offer we made some time back."

Via Digital, the platform favoured by Spain's conservative government, has offered 130 billion pesetas ($839.3 million) to Audiovisual Sport for non-exclusive access to its broadcast rights to all Spanish soccer league and cup matches for six years.

But Canal Satelite paid 15 billion pesetas for exclusive rights for the 1998/99 season through 2003. The platform contends it also holds rights for the upcoming season through the Spanish unit of Canal Plus pay television channel.
A lower court judge ruled on August 14 that Canal Satelite could not prove its claim to the upcoming season matches.

Telefonica, meanwhile, has tried to wrest control of the football rights for Via Digital by buying 25 percent of private television station Antena 3 and control of its 40 percent stake in Audiovisual Sport.

Industry sources said Telefonica's acquisition of Antena 3, which was a Canal Satelite partner, and its entrance in Audiovisual Sport capital had forced the rival platform to negotiate the distribution of football rights.

"It seems that there is a certain willingness to negotiate the football rights, but it's still early to talk about a true convergence of positions between the two platforms," one source close to the parties said.
Earlier in the month, Canal Satelite challenged the Antena 3 purchase before the European Commission as an abuse of Telefonica's dominant position in the sector.

The Commission then warned the Spanish telecoms operator against going ahead with its acquisition without getting EU approval. Telefonica defied the Commission, saying it was a domestic rather than a European competition issue.
Telefonica effectively assumed control of Antena 3 on Monday. EU competition officials said on Tuesday they would meet Telefonica representatives in the next few days. ($ = 154.8 Spanish Pesetas)
